challenges.name: status-codes-errors-quiz
challenges.title: Read the error responses
challenges.description: Three statements about status codes and error bodies in Rice Rocket's order API. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Ask what a client does with the status code before it reads the body: a mobile app's HTTP client decides success or failure from the code alone.
Separate the two questions an API answers about a caller: do I know who you are, and are you allowed to do this?
Read the contract text quoted with the evidence: it decides which of two plausible codes is right for this API.

questions.question:
A test for ordering from a closed restaurant, and what the API answered:

```python
def test_order_closed_restaurant(api):
    response = api.post("/orders", json={**ORDER, "restaurant_id": 17})
    assert response.status_code < 500
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "restaurant closed"}
```

Statement: "The test is right to pass: 200 is not a server error, so the API handled the request correctly."
questions.explanation: False. The order was not created, but the status says it was: every HTTP client, retry layer and dashboard treats 200 as success, and the courier app showed "order placed". The contract asks for 409 with a problem type for a closed restaurant, and the test should assert that exact code. `< 500` only proves the server did not crash. The misconception is that the body's text is part of what clients check.

questions.question:
A courier (valid token, role `courier`) calls an admin endpoint:

```text
GET /admin/payouts
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... (valid, role=courier)

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
```

Statement: "401 is the right answer, because the courier is not authorized to see payouts."
questions.explanation: False. Despite its name, 401 means the request is not authenticated (no or invalid credentials), and it tells the client to log in again; the app would sign the courier out. The token is valid and identifies the courier, who simply lacks the permission: that is 403 Forbidden. The misconception comes from the reason phrase "Unauthorized".

questions.question:
Rice Rocket's contract says: "400 when the body is not valid JSON; 422 when it is valid JSON that breaks a rule of the schema". Two requests:

```text
POST /orders   {"quantity": 2,           -> 400
POST /orders   {"quantity": 0}            -> 422
```

Statement: "Under this contract both answers are right, and a test that accepts any 4xx would miss an API that swaps them."
questions.explanation: True. The first body cannot be parsed, the second parses but breaks `minimum: 1`, and the contract gives them different codes; clients use the difference (a 400 is a bug in the client, a 422 is a user input to show next to the field). A test asserting `400 <= status < 500` passes when the API swaps them. Some APIs use 400 for both; what matters is that the contract says which and the test asserts it exactly.

challenges.name: fix-response-assertions
challenges.title: Fix the response assertions
challenges.description: Every API test of Rice Rocket goes through `check_response(expected, response)`, and the old version let three bugs reach production: a 400 where the contract says 422 ("same class"), a 200 carrying `{"error": ...}`, and error bodies in several shapes. It also failed correct responses whose content type carried `; charset=utf-8` or whose field errors came in another order. The editor holds `assertions.py` with its checks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are the old buggy checks. Fill every line so the helper follows the rules in the file's docstring: the exact status, no error body on a success, RFC 9457 problem details for errors (media type, members, status, type, field pointers in any order) and Retry-After on 429.
hints: For each check, think of a correct response that it must accept and a broken one it must reject; the old checks fail one of the two.
Look at how the status is compared, how the Content-Type header is split before comparing (parameters, case), and whether the field pointers are compared as lists or as sets.

A similar check for a JSON success response: `media = headers.get("content-type", "").split(";")[0].strip().lower()` and `assert media == "application/json"`, so `application/json; charset=utf-8` passes and `text/html` fails.
